question: Before loading or unloading a vehicle carrying hazardous materials, what must a driver do first?
choice_a: Turn on hazard flashers only
choice_c: Set the parking brake and make sure the vehicle will not move
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states before loading or unloading, set the parking brake and make sure the vehicle will not move.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements

question: Is it legal to move a vehicle carrying leaking hazardous materials packages?
choice_a: No, it is illegal to move a vehicle with leaking hazardous materials
choice_c: Yes, as long as the windows are open
choice_d: Yes, if the leak is minor
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states it is illegal to move a vehicle with leaking hazardous materials.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements

question: What must be done to containers of hazardous materials to prevent movement of the packages during transportation?
choice_a: They must be placed loose in the trailer
choice_b: They must be wrapped only in plastic
choice_c: They must be stacked with the heaviest items on top
choice_d: They must be braced/secured against movement
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states containers of hazardous materials must be braced to prevent movement of the packages during transportation, and all packages must be secured.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements

question: Around which hazard classes must a driver never allow smoking while loading or unloading?
choice_a: Only Class 1 (Explosives)
choice_b: Class 1, Division 2.1, Class 3, Class 4, and Class 5
choice_c: All classes except Class 9
choice_d: Class 6, Class 7, Class 8, and Class 9 only
explanation: Section 9.4.1 lists Class 1 (Explosives), Division 2.1 (Flammable Gas), Class 3 (Flammable Liquids), Class 4 (Flammable Solids), and Class 5 (Oxidizers) as classes around which smoking is never allowed during loading/unloading.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, No Smoking

question: Unless a driver has read all related rules, cargo heaters (including automatic cargo heater/air conditioner units) generally should not be used when the cargo space holds which classes?
choice_a: All hazard classes equally
choice_c: Class 1 (Explosives), Division 2.1 (Flammable Gas), and Class 3 (Flammable Liquids)
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states the rules usually forbid use of cargo heaters when loading Class 1, Division 2.1, and Class 3 materials unless all related rules have been read.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, Cargo Heater Rules

question: Which hazard classes cannot be transported as overhang or tailgate loads and generally must be in a closed cargo space unless fire- and water-resistant or covered by a fire- and water-resistant tarp?
choice_a: Class 8 (Corrosives) only
choice_c: Class 2 (Compressed Gases) only
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states you cannot have overhang or tailgate loads of Class 1, Class 4, and Class 5 materials; they must be loaded into a closed cargo space unless all packages are fire and water resistant, or covered with a fire and water resistant tarp.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, Use Closed Cargo Space

question: Before loading or unloading explosives, what must a driver do with the engine?
choice_a: Turn it off
choice_c: Rev it briefly to check operation
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states to turn your engine off before loading or unloading any explosives, then check the cargo space.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, Class 1 (Explosives) Materials

question: What type of floor lining is required for a cargo space carrying Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives?
choice_a: Rubberized carpet only
choice_b: A tight floor with a non-metallic material or non-ferrous metal liner
choice_c: Stainless steel plating
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states the floors must be tight and the liner must be either non-metallic material or non-ferrous metal when loading Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, Class 1 (Explosives) Materials

question: When is it acceptable to transfer Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives from one vehicle to another on a public roadway?
choice_a: Only at night
choice_b: Only in an emergency, after setting out red warning reflectors, flags, or electric lanterns
choice_c: Never, under any circumstances including emergencies
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states not to transfer Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives from one vehicle to another on a public roadway except in an emergency, and if safety requires it, set out red warning reflectors, flags, or electric lanterns.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, Class 1 (Explosives) Materials

question: Should a driver ever transport a package of explosives that shows dampness or an oily stain?
choice_a: Yes, if placed at the rear of the trailer
choice_c: No, never transport a damaged, damp, or oily-stained explosives package
choice_d: Yes, if the damage looks minor
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states never transport damaged packages of explosives, and not to take a package that shows any dampness or oily stain.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, Class 1 (Explosives) Materials

question: If a vehicle carrying compressed gas cylinders has no racks, what must the cargo space floor be like, and how must the cylinders be positioned?
choice_a: The floor must be flat, and cylinders held upright, or horizontal only if designed with the relief valve in the vapor space
choice_b: The floor must be carpeted, and cylinders may lie in any direction
choice_c: The floor must be insulated, and cylinders wrapped in blankets
choice_d: The floor must be ramped, and cylinders secured with tape
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states if the vehicle doesn't have racks, the floor must be flat, cylinders held upright or in racks/boxes, and may only be loaded horizontally if designed so the relief valve is in the vapor space.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, Class 2 (Compressed Gases)

question: Where must a driver never load a package labeled POISON or POISON INHALATION HAZARD?
choice_a: On the top shelf of the trailer
choice_c: Near the vehicle's fuel tank only
choice_d: In the driver's cab or sleeper, or with food for human or animal consumption
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states never load a package labeled POISON or POISON INHALATION HAZARD in the driver's cab or sleeper or with food material for human or animal consumption.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, Division 2.3/6.1 Materials

question: Class 4 and Class 5 materials that become unstable and dangerous when wet must be:
choice_a: Kept moist to prevent static buildup
choice_c: Kept dry while in transit and during loading and unloading
choice_d: Loaded together with corrosive liquids for balance
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states Class 4 and 5 materials which become unstable and dangerous when wet must be kept dry while in transit and during loading and unloading.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, Class 4/5 Materials

question: What is the maximum total transport index of all Class 7 (Radioactive) packages allowed together in a single vehicle?
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states the total transport index of all packages in a single vehicle must not exceed 50.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, Class 7 (Radioactive) Materials

question: What does a Class 7 package's "transport index" tell a driver?
choice_a: The exact weight of the package in kilograms
choice_b: The number of days the package can be stored
choice_c: The maximum speed the vehicle may travel
choice_d: The degree of control needed during transportation, including how close the package may be to people, animals, or film
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states the transport index tells the degree of control needed during transportation and how close Class 7 materials can be loaded to people, animals, or film.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, Class 7 (Radioactive) Materials

question: Nitric acid must never be loaded in what position relative to other products?
choice_a: In the front of the trailer only
choice_c: Below any other product
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states do not load nitric acid above any other product.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, Class 8 (Corrosive) Materials

question: According to the Do Not Load table, Division 6.1 or 2.3 poison materials must not be loaded in the same vehicle with:
choice_a: Paper products
choice_c: Empty pallets
choice_d: Animal or human food, unless the poison package is over-packed in an approved way
explanation: Figure 9.9, the Do Not Load Table, states Division 6.1 or 2.3 poison-labeled material must not be loaded with animal or human food unless the poison package is over-packed in an approved way.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4 Loading and Unloading, Figure 9.9, Do Not Load Table

question: According to the Do Not Load table, Division 2.3 (Poisonous gas, Zone A) or Division 6.1 (Poison) liquids PGI Zone A must not be loaded with which of these?
choice_a: Only combustible liquids
choice_b: Division 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 Explosives, Division 5.1 Oxidizers, Class 3 Flammable Liquids, Class 8 Corrosive Liquids, or Division 5.2 Organic Peroxides
choice_c: Only ORM-D materials
explanation: Figure 9.9, the Do Not Load Table, lists Division 1.1/1.2/1.3 Explosives, Division 5.1 Oxidizers, Class 3 Flammable Liquids, Class 8 Corrosive Liquids, and Division 5.2 Organic Peroxides as materials that cannot be loaded with Division 2.3 Zone A gas or Division 6.1 PGI Zone A poison liquids.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4 Loading and Unloading, Figure 9.9, Do Not Load Table

question: Charged storage batteries must never be loaded in the same vehicle with which explosives?
choice_a: Division 1.1
choice_c: Division 6.2
explanation: Figure 9.9, the Do Not Load Table, lists Division 1.1 explosives as materials that must not be loaded with charged storage batteries.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4 Loading and Unloading, Figure 9.9, Do Not Load Table

question: Division 6.1 cyanides or cyanide mixtures (such as Silver Cyanide or Sodium Cyanide) must not be loaded with which materials, because contact could release hydrocyanic acid?
choice_a: Foodstuffs only
choice_b: Acids, corrosive materials, or other acidic materials
choice_c: Flammable gases only
explanation: Figure 9.9, the Do Not Load Table, states cyanides or cyanide mixtures must not be loaded with acids, corrosive materials, or other acidic materials that could release hydrocyanic acid.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4 Loading and Unloading, Figure 9.9, Do Not Load Table

question: What is the key difference between a cargo tank and a portable tank?
choice_a: There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
choice_b: A cargo tank is always smaller than a portable tank
choice_c: A cargo tank only carries gases, while a portable tank only carries liquids
choice_d: A cargo tank is permanently attached to a vehicle, while a portable tank is loaded/unloaded off the vehicle and then placed onto it for transportation
explanation: Section 9.5 states cargo tanks are bulk packaging permanently attached to a vehicle and remain on the vehicle when loaded and unloaded, while portable tanks are loaded or unloaded off the vehicle and then put on a vehicle for transportation.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5 Bulk Packaging Marking, Loading and Unloading

question: What are the two most common types of cargo tanks mentioned in the manual, used for liquids and gases respectively?
choice_a: MC307 and MC338
choice_c: DOT-111 and DOT-117
explanation: Section 9.5 states the most common cargo tanks are MC306 for liquids and MC331 for gases.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5 Bulk Packaging Marking, Loading and Unloading

question: Identification numbers on portable tanks, cargo tanks, and other bulk packaging must be displayed as black numbers of what size, on orange panels, placards, or a white diamond-shaped background?
choice_a: 50 mm numbers
choice_c: 250 mm numbers
explanation: Section 9.5.1 states the rules require black 100 mm (3.9 inch) numbers on orange panels, placards, or a white diamond-shaped background.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.1 Markings

question: On a portable tank with a capacity of more than 1,000 gallons, how tall must the letters of the shipping name be?
choice_a: At least six inches
choice_c: At least two inches
explanation: Section 9.5.1 states the letters of the shipping name must be at least two inches tall on portable tanks with capacities of more than 1,000 gallons.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.1 Markings

question: The person watching the loading or unloading of a cargo tank must be alert, have a clear view of the tank, and stay within how many feet of it?
choice_a: 50 feet
choice_c: 25 feet
explanation: Section 9.5.2 states the person watching loading or unloading must be alert, have a clear view of the cargo tank, and be within 25 feet of the tank.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.2 Tank Loading

question: Before moving a cargo tank of hazardous materials, no matter how small the amount, what must be done?
choice_a: Close all manholes and valves
choice_c: Notify local police
explanation: Section 9.5.2 states close all manholes and valves before moving a tank of hazardous materials, no matter how small the amount in the tank or how short the distance.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.2 Tank Loading

question: Before loading or unloading flammable liquids into a cargo tank, what should be done with the engine, and what must be done to the tank before opening the filling hole?
choice_a: Fill the tank to the maximum level first
choice_b: Leave the engine running for the entire process
choice_c: Disconnect the battery entirely
choice_d: Turn off the engine (unless needed for a pump), and ground the tank correctly
explanation: Section 9.5.3 states to turn off the engine before loading or unloading flammable liquids (only run it if needed to operate a pump) and to ground a cargo tank correctly before filling it through an open filling hole.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.3 Flammable Liquids

question: When trailers and semi-trailers are uncoupled from the power unit during compressed gas loading/unloading, what must be done to them?
choice_a: They must be disconnected from all placards
choice_c: They must be left on an incline
choice_d: They must always be chocked to prevent motion
explanation: Section 9.5.4 states to always chock trailers and semi-trailers to prevent motion when uncoupled from the power unit.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.4 Compressed Gas

question: A vehicle carrying Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives must never be parked within how many feet of the traveled part of the road?
choice_a: Twenty feet
choice_c: One hundred feet
explanation: Section 9.6.1 states never park with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives within five feet of the traveled part of the road.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.1 Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

question: Except for brief operational necessities like fueling, a vehicle with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives must not be parked within how many feet of a bridge, tunnel, building, place where people gather, or an open fire?
choice_a: 1,000 feet
choice_c: 500 feet
explanation: Section 9.6.1 states except for short periods needed for operation necessities, do not park within 300 feet of a bridge, tunnel, building, a place where people gather, or an open fire.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.1 Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

question: What is a "safe haven" as described in the manual?
choice_a: A repair facility certified for hazmat vehicles
choice_b: A designated rest stop for all commercial vehicles
choice_c: A fenced area at any truck stop
choice_d: An approved place for parking unattended vehicles loaded with explosives, usually designated by local authorities
explanation: Section 9.6.1 defines a safe haven as an approved place for parking unattended vehicles loaded with explosives, with designation usually made by local authorities.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.1 Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

question: A driver may park a placarded vehicle not laden with explosives within five feet of the traveled roadway only if:
choice_a: The driver holds a special permit
choice_c: Work requires it, and it is done only briefly
explanation: Section 9.6.2 states a driver may park a placarded vehicle not laden with explosives within five feet of the traveled roadway only if work requires it, and only briefly.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.2 Parking a Placarded Vehicle Not Transporting Explosives

question: When attending a parked placarded vehicle, the attendant must be in the vehicle awake and not in the sleeper berth, or within how many feet of the vehicle with it in clear view?
choice_a: 500 feet
choice_c: 300 feet
explanation: Section 9.6.3 states the person attending a placarded vehicle must be in the vehicle, awake, and not in the sleeper berth, or within 100 feet of the vehicle and have it within clear view.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.3 Attending Parked Vehicles

question: Near a tank used for Class 3 (Flammable Liquids) or Division 2.1 (Flammable Gas), whether loaded or empty, what type of warning device must a driver never use?
choice_a: Burning signals such as flares or fuses
choice_c: Hazard flashers
explanation: Section 9.6.4 states never use burning signals, such as flares or fuses, around a tank used for Class 3 or Division 2.1, or a vehicle loaded with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.4 No Flares!

question: If transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, what must a driver have and follow while en route?
choice_a: A fuel efficiency log
choice_c: A verbal agreement with the shipper
explanation: Section 9.6.5 states if transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, you must have a written route plan and follow that plan.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.5 Route Restrictions

question: When transporting placarded radioactive materials, who must choose the safest route and inform the driver about the materials and route plan?
choice_a: The consignee
choice_c: The driver alone
explanation: Section 9.6.5 states a carrier must choose the safest route to transport placarded radioactive materials and must tell the driver about the materials and show the route plan.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.5 Route Restrictions

question: A driver must not smoke within how many feet of a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 (flammable liquids) or Division 2.1 (gases)?
choice_a: 100 feet
choice_c: 25 feet
explanation: Section 9.6.6 states do not smoke within 25 feet of a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 or Division 2.1.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.6 No Smoking

question: Before fueling a motor vehicle containing hazardous materials, what must the driver do with the engine, and who must be at the nozzle?
choice_a: Leave the engine running to power the pump, unattended
choice_b: Turn off the engine and lock the fuel door
choice_c: Idle the engine and step away
choice_d: Turn off the engine, and someone must always be at the nozzle controlling fuel flow
explanation: Section 9.6.7 states to turn off the engine before fueling a motor vehicle containing hazardous materials, and someone must always be at the nozzle, controlling fuel flow.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.7 Refuel with Engine Off

question: The power unit of placarded vehicles must have a fire extinguisher with what UL rating or more?
choice_c: 10 B:C
explanation: Section 9.6.8 states the power unit of placarded vehicles must have a fire extinguisher with a UL rating of 10 B:C or more.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.8 10 B C Fire Extinguisher

question: When behind the wheel, where must a driver keep hazardous materials shipping papers?
choice_a: In the trailer with the cargo
choice_c: Within reach with the seat belt fastened, or in a pouch on the driver's door
explanation: Section 9.6.10 states when behind the wheel, keep shipping papers within reach with the seat belt fastened, or in a pouch on the driver's door.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.10 Where to Keep Shipping Papers and Emergency Response Information

question: A carrier must give a driver transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives written instructions plus a copy of which federal regulations part?
choice_a: FMCSR Part 350
choice_c: 49 CFR Part 100
explanation: Section 9.6.10 states a carrier must give each driver transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives a copy of Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations (FMCSR), Part 397, along with written instructions.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.10 Where to Keep Shipping Papers and Emergency Response Information

question: A driver transporting chlorine in cargo tanks must have what special equipment in the vehicle?
choice_a: Extra placards only
choice_b: A hazmat suit and self-contained breathing apparatus
choice_c: A fire-resistant blanket only
choice_d: An approved gas mask and an emergency kit for controlling leaks in dome cover plate fittings
explanation: Section 9.6.11 states a driver transporting chlorine in cargo tanks must have an approved gas mask and an emergency kit for controlling leaks in dome cover plate fittings on the cargo tank.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.11 Equipment for Chlorine

question: A vehicle that is placarded, carries any amount of chlorine, or has cargo tanks (loaded or empty) used for hazardous materials must stop how far before a railroad crossing?
choice_a: 50 to 100 feet
choice_c: 100 to 200 feet
explanation: Section 9.6.12 states you must stop 15 to 50 feet before the nearest rail, proceeding only when sure no train is coming.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.12 Stop before Railroad Crossings

question: At the scene of a crash or incident involving hazardous materials, what is a driver's job?
choice_a: Keep people away, limit the spread of material if it can be done safely, and communicate the danger to emergency responders
choice_b: Attempt to clean up the spill personally before help arrives
choice_c: Move the vehicle immediately regardless of conditions
choice_d: Leave the scene to alert the shipper in person
explanation: Section 9.7.2 states a driver's job at the scene is to keep people away from the scene, limit the spread of material only if safe, and communicate the danger to emergency responders.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.2 Crashes/Incidents

question: If trailer doors feel hot after a possible cargo fire, what should a driver do?
choice_a: Open them immediately to check for damage
choice_b: Not open the doors, since opening them lets in air and may make the fire flare up
choice_c: Remove the placards before opening
choice_d: Spray water through the door seams
explanation: Section 9.7.3 states feel trailer doors to see if they are hot before opening them; if hot, do not open the doors because opening them lets in air and may make the fire flare up.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.3 Fires

question: If hazardous materials are spilling from a vehicle, what is the recommended sequence of actions?
choice_a: Park it, secure the area, stay there, and call for help or send someone else for help
choice_b: Attempt to transfer the load to another vehicle immediately
choice_c: Continue to the destination and report upon arrival
choice_d: Drive to the nearest phone as quickly as possible
explanation: Section 9.7.3 lists the checklist for a spill as: park it, secure the area, stay there, and call for help or send someone else for help.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.3 Fires

question: Should a driver continue driving with hazardous materials leaking from the vehicle in order to reach a phone or truck stop?
choice_a: Yes, if the leak is small
choice_b: Yes, as long as the windows stay closed
choice_c: No, never continue driving with leaking hazardous materials in order to find help
explanation: Section 9.7.3 states never continue driving with hazardous materials leaking from your vehicle in order to find a phone, truck stop, help, or similar reason.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.3 Fires

question: In a breakdown or collision involving Class 1 explosives, if explosives must be removed before separating the vehicles, how far away from the vehicles and occupied buildings should they be placed?
choice_a: At least 20 feet
choice_c: At least 500 feet
explanation: Section 9.7.4 states to remove all explosives before separating vehicles involved in a collision and place the explosives at least 200 feet from the vehicles and occupied buildings.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.4 Responses to Specific Hazards, Class 1 (Explosives)

question: After a Class 8 (Corrosive) material spill, what must be done to parts of the vehicle exposed to the corrosive liquid?
choice_a: Wiped with a dry cloth only
choice_c: Covered with sand and left overnight
choice_d: Left as is until the next scheduled wash
explanation: Section 9.7.4 states parts of the vehicle exposed to a corrosive liquid must be thoroughly washed with water.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.4 Responses to Specific Hazards, Class 8 (Corrosive) Materials

question: If a Class 7 (Radioactive) package is spilled or an internal container might be damaged, what should a driver do?
choice_a: Not touch or inhale the material, and not use the vehicle until it is cleaned and checked with a survey meter
choice_b: Bury the package at the roadside
choice_c: Continue the trip and report at the next scheduled stop
choice_d: Immediately hose down the vehicle with water
explanation: Section 9.7.4 states if there is a spill or an internal container might be damaged, do not touch or inhale the material, and do not use the vehicle until it is cleaned and checked with a survey meter.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.4 Responses to Specific Hazards, Class 7 (Radioactive Materials)

question: Which of the following is one of the thresholds requiring notification of the National Response Center after a hazardous materials incident?
choice_a: The shipment is delayed by more than one hour
choice_b: A person is killed, or estimated property damage exceeds $50,000
choice_c: The driver receives a traffic citation
explanation: Section 9.7.5 lists a death and property damage exceeding $50,000 among the events that require notification of the National Response Center.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.5 Required Notification

question: What is the toll-free phone number for the National Response Center given in the manual?
explanation: Section 9.7.5 lists the National Response Center's 24-hour toll-free number as (800) 424-8802.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.5 Required Notification

question: What is CHEMTREC, and what is its toll-free number given in the manual?
choice_a: The Chemical Transportation Emergency Center, providing technical information about hazardous materials, at (800) 424-9300
choice_b: A private insurance hotline for cargo claims
choice_c: A government agency that issues hazmat endorsements, at (800) 424-8802
choice_d: A weather service used for hazmat routing
explanation: Section 9.7.5 describes CHEMTREC (the Chemical Transportation Emergency Center) in Washington as providing emergency personnel with technical information about hazardous materials, at (800) 424-9300.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.5 Required Notification

question: According to the glossary, what is the definition of "hazard class"?
choice_a: The driver's endorsement classification
choice_b: The type of placard displayed on the vehicle
choice_c: The category of hazard assigned to a hazardous material under the definitional criteria of Part 173 and the Sec. 172.101 Table
choice_d: The weight class of the transporting vehicle
explanation: Section 9.8 defines hazard class as the category of hazard assigned to a hazardous material under the defining criteria of Part 173 and the Sec. 172.101 Table.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.8 Hazardous Materials Glossary

question: According to the glossary, what is a "consignee"?
choice_a: The person who packages the hazardous material
choice_b: The business or person to whom a shipment is delivered
choice_c: The government agency that inspects shipments
choice_d: The insurance company covering the shipment
explanation: Section 9.8 defines consignee as the business or person to whom a shipment is delivered.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.8 Hazardous Materials Glossary

question: According to the glossary, what does "N.O.S." stand for?
choice_a: Not otherwise specified
choice_c: National Ordinance Standard
explanation: Section 9.8 defines N.O.S. as "Not otherwise specified."
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.8 Hazardous Materials Glossary

question: According to the glossary, what is a "reportable quantity (RQ)"?
choice_a: The maximum weight a truck may legally carry
choice_b: The number of placards required on a vehicle
choice_c: The quantity specified in Column 2 of the Appendix to Sec. 172.101 for a material identified in Column 1
choice_d: The minimum quantity exempt from all regulation
explanation: Section 9.8 defines reportable quantity (RQ) as the quantity specified in Column 2 of the Appendix to Sec. 172.101 for any material identified in Column 1 of the Appendix.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.8 Hazardous Materials Glossary

question: According to the glossary, what is the definition of a "shipping paper"?
choice_a: A shipping order, bill of lading, manifest, or other shipping document serving a similar purpose, prepared in accordance with subpart C of part 172
choice_c: A receipt confirming delivery signed by the consignee
choice_d: Any document listing the driver's hours of service
explanation: Section 9.8 defines shipping paper as a shipping order, bill of lading, manifest, or other shipping document serving a similar purpose, prepared according to subpart C of part 172.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.8 Hazardous Materials Glossary

question: According to the glossary, what is a "portable tank" (as distinguished from a cargo tank)?
choice_a: A tank permanently welded to the vehicle chassis
choice_b: Any tank of any size used to store fuel for the transport vehicle
choice_c: Bulk packaging designed primarily to be loaded onto, or temporarily attached to, a transport vehicle or ship, equipped with skids or mountings to facilitate handling by mechanical means
choice_d: A cylinder with a water capacity of 1,000 pounds or less
explanation: Section 9.8 defines portable tank as bulk packaging (except a cylinder having a water capacity of 1,000 pounds or less) designed primarily to be loaded onto or temporarily attached to a transport vehicle or ship, equipped with skids, mountings, or accessories to facilitate handling by mechanical means.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.8 Hazardous Materials Glossary

question: According to the glossary, what is the definition of "proper shipping name"?
choice_a: Any commonly used trade name for the product
choice_c: The name of the hazardous material shown in Roman print (not italics) in Sec. 172.101
choice_d: The name assigned by the driver on the trip log
explanation: Section 9.8 defines proper shipping name as the name of the hazardous materials shown in Roman print (not italics) in Sec. 172.101.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.8 Hazardous Materials Glossary
